name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,400

clue.text: Back of car missing special sticker?

indicators.note: the back of something is its final part, which is the part that is to go
missing means absent, so the car word appears without its end letter

blocks.note: a limo is a long luxury car
a pet project or pet subject is a special favourite

explanation.surface: A motorist finds that a special sticker has fallen off the back of the car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back of car missing' reads as the car having lost its back end: LIMO without its last letter. 'missing' is part of that instruction, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A limpet clings so firmly to rocks that its name is used for anything or anyone that sticks fast.

clue.text: Nothing unaccounted for on one's trolley, presumably?

blocks.note: first meaning: every item is present and counted
second meaning: sane, the opposite of the slang 'off one's trolley' meaning mad

explanation.surface: A shopper checks that every item is still sitting on the supermarket trolley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off one's trolley' is British slang for crazy, so being on it, presumably, means mentally sound. The surface makes it a literal shopping trolley.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both that every item is present and, of a person, being mentally alert and sane.

clue.text: Discovered two - not put about so far

indicators.note: dis-covered means with the covering stripped off, so only the letters within the outer ones are kept
put about means turned to face the other way, so the kept letters are read from end to start

blocks.note: the three words run together, ignoring the dash, with the outer T at each end stripped off

explanation.surface: Two things have come to light, with one item not yet put about.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip the T from each end of 'two not put' and read what is left backwards. The dash is only punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: Up to now and so far both mean until the present moment, an idiomatic pair of synonyms.

clue.text: It's chewed by dog after picking up clodhopper

indicators.note: something chewed is mangled out of shape, so those letters are jumbled
in a down entry, picked up means lifted, so the dog word runs from bottom to top
held by the dog means gripped inside the dog word

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A dog chews something it has just picked up, perhaps an old boot.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the dog reads upwards; 'after' only joins the definition to the wordplay, and a clodhopper here is a person, not a boot.
explanation.definitionFit: A clodhopper is a clumsy country bumpkin, which is what a rustic means as a noun: an unsophisticated rural person.

clue.text: Flight-path modified heading off to Etruria

indicators.note: with its heading off, the short word loses its first letter
something modified has been changed, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the little word without its first letter
the ancient region of Italy, taken as written

explanation.surface: An airline has changed the flight path heading off to Etruria in ancient Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: An air route is the corridor an aircraft follows between places, the same as its planned flight path.

clue.text: Magnum, perhaps, hard to charge with a litre bottle

indicators.note: charging something means loading it, so the detective word is filled with the letter for hard

blocks.note: Magnum PI was the private investigator of the TV series
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for litre

explanation.surface: A magnum, the big wine bottle, is hard to fill with a single litre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Magnum' suggests a large wine bottle, but here it is Thomas Magnum, the TV private eye. H goes inside PI, then A and L follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A phial is a small glass bottle, usually for medicine or perfume, so bottle is its straightforward category.

clue.text: Chairs put out around club in preparation for patients

indicators.note: chairs put out are spread about rather than in rows, so these letters are rearranged
around means surrounding, so the jumbled letters enclose the club word

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be jumbled
a mace is a heavy club used as a weapon

explanation.surface: Chairs are set out in a club room, getting ready for patients to arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of CHAIRS PUT splits around MACE. 'in' joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pharmaceutics is the science of preparing and dispensing medicines, the making-ready of drugs that patients take.

clue.text: The old man on intermission

definitions.note: a noun, matched by the verbal noun 'pausing'

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father, one's old man
on drugs means using them

explanation.surface: Dad has gone out during the interval at the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' looks like a link word, but it supplies the second part: someone on drugs is using.
explanation.definitionFit: An intermission is a pause in a performance, and pausing names that act of temporarily stopping.

clue.text: Lonely husbands not fully understanding wise words, unfortunately

indicators.note: not fully means incomplete, so the understanding word loses its last letter
something gone unfortunately has gone wrong, so the letters fall out of their order

blocks.note: a grasp of a subject is an understanding of it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lonely husbands fail to grasp the wise words offered to them, sadly.
explanation.walkthrough: GRASP loses its P, and those letters are jumbled with WISE WORDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Grass widowers are husbands left alone at home while their wives are away, hence lonely men temporarily without partners.

clue.text: Not much to write about a parliamentarian collar

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the small-amount word wraps the other letters

blocks.note: a jot is a tiny amount, and to jot is to write briefly
taken as written
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A note about an MP's choice of collar would hardly fill a page.
explanation.walkthrough: A jampot collar is the tall, round clerical collar worn by some clergy, so the definition is less obvious than it looks.
explanation.definitionFit: A jampot is the nickname for a high round clerical collar, shaped like the neck of a jam jar.

clue.text: In error, leave to escape the onset of war?

blocks.note: a sum that is out is wrong
leave from work is a break

explanation.surface: A soldier mistakenly takes leave to get away before a war begins.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions surround the wordplay: an outbreak is a prison escape and also the start of hostilities.
explanation.definitionFit: An outbreak is a breakout from captivity and also the sudden start of something like war or disease.

clue.text: Someone covering Aintree? It's routine

blocks.note: cryptic meaning: a reporter assigned to a racecourse would cover the matters of that course
straight meaning: something expected, done as normal practice

explanation.walkthrough: Aintree is the Liverpool racecourse where the Grand National is run; a journalist covering it deals with matters of the course.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done as a matter of course happens naturally and expectedly, which is what routine means.

clue.text: I doubt he eats very quickly

blocks.note: first meaning: one who mocks and doubts, saying 'I doubt it'
second meaning: one who gobbles food greedily

explanation.surface: Someone is sceptical that a certain man really bolts his food.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a sentence it is a doubt about someone's eating; split, 'I doubt' describes a sceptic and 'he eats very quickly' describes a gobbler.
explanation.definitionFit: To scoff is both to jeer with disbelief and, informally, to wolf down food, so the noun names both people.

clue.text: Some cauliflower cheese, 75% reduced in store

indicators.note: keeping three quarters of a four-letter cheese means its final letter goes
in means placed inside, so the reduced word sits within the trimmed cheese

blocks.note: feta is a Greek cheese
a reduced price is a lower one

explanation.surface: A cauliflower cheese, mostly marked down, sits on a store shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some cauliflower cheese' looks like one dish, but the definition stops at 'cauliflower'. FETA loses a quarter to give FET, which holds LOWER.
explanation.definitionFit: A floweret, or floret, is one of the small clustered heads that make up a cauliflower, so a portion of it.

clue.text: Topless online business service made permanent selection?

indicators.note: topless means with the top removed, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: LinkedIn is the professional networking website

explanation.surface: A business website without its header has been chosen for good.
explanation.walkthrough: A provisional team selection pencilled in is later inked in once it is final.
explanation.definitionFit: Inked in means written in ink, so confirmed and fixed, as with a choice no longer provisional.

clue.text: "Gift" turning up on aircraft containing cocaine considered unimportant?

indicators.note: turning up in a down entry means flipping so it reads from the bottom upwards
containing means holding inside, so the aircraft word wraps the drug letter

blocks.note: a boon is a blessing or gift
a jet is an aircraft
C is the slang abbreviation for cocaine

explanation.surface: A gift turns up on a plane carrying cocaine, which is treated as no big deal.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so the reversed gift sits atop the aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: If money is no object it is not a consideration, so the phrase marks something as unimportant.

clue.text: Under legal obligation regarding invalid no doubt

indicators.note: an invalid argument is broken, so these letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lawyer sounds certain about whether a contract is void.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no doubt' looks like the definition, since the answer can mean certain, but it is the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To be bound to do something is to be required by contract or law, which is a legal obligation.

clue.text: Unbalanced, so not in for a bit ...

blocks.note: out of stock means not in stock
pro is Latin for in favour of
a portion is a bit of something

explanation.surface: Someone feeling off balance is not taking part for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on to 20 across, which picks up the thread.
explanation.definitionFit: Something out of proportion has its parts in the wrong relative sizes, so it is lopsided or unbalanced.

clue.text: In spin, Lion's caught by Hammer

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the lion part sits within the spin letters
something caught by the lion is held inside it, so the multiplication letter goes within

blocks.note: PR, public relations, is spin
Leo is the lion of the zodiac
X is the multiplication sign, read as by, as in two by four

explanation.surface: A spinning lion is caught out by a West Ham player, a Hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is not a link but the times sign, as in two by four. West Ham footballers are nicknamed the Hammers, which hides the doctor's tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A plexor is the small rubber-headed hammer a doctor uses to tap the body in percussion tests.

clue.text: What to do if criterion is satisfied in sound test? Pass

indicators.note: a sound test is a listening check, so the phrase is judged by how it is heard

blocks.clueFragment: What to do if criterion is satisfied
blocks.note: you put a tick against a box whose criterion is met

explanation.surface: An examiner explains how to mark a test as passed once each criterion is met.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' sits apart at the end after the question mark, looking like part of the exam story.
explanation.definitionFit: A ticket is a pass granting entry or travel, as with a bus pass or a free admission voucher.

clue.text: ... -1 after the round, the number for the next round?

definitions.text: the number for the next round?

blocks.clueFragment: ... -1 after the round, the number for the next round?
blocks.note: surface reading: carrying on from 17 across, a golfer's scorecard figure after finishing
setter's reading: the entry's own number minus one

blocks.clueFragment: after the round, the number for the next round?
blocks.note: setter's reading: golfers retire to the clubhouse bar, jokingly named as the extra hole after eighteen, to buy the next round of drinks

explanation.walkthrough: This is 20 across, and 20 minus 1 is the answer. The clubhouse bar is called the nineteenth hole, where a round of golf ends and a round of drinks begins.
explanation.definitionFit: The golf club bar is nicknamed by this number, as the hole played after the regular eighteen, where drinks are bought.

clue.text: Japanese duty officer's crucial manoeuvre

blocks.note: J is the abbreviation for Japanese
OC is the officer commanding, the one on charge of a unit
a key point is a crucial one

explanation.surface: A Japanese officer on duty makes a vital tactical move.
explanation.walkthrough: Jockeying for position is manoeuvring to gain an advantage.
explanation.definitionFit: To jockey is to manoeuvre skilfully for advantage, as riders do when jostling for position in a race.

clue.text: Make sure noisette has no trace of nuts before distributing

indicators.note: no trace of a word means not even its first letter, so that initial is struck out
distributing spreads things around, so the remaining letters are dealt out in a new order

blocks.note: a noisette is a small round piece of meat, or a hazelnut chocolate
the trace of the word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A chef checks that a nut-free noisette has no traces of nuts before serving.
explanation.walkthrough: One N comes out of NOISETTE, and the other seven letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To see to it is to attend to something so that it happens, which is making sure.

clue.text: It's played on board ship by chemical engineer

blocks.note: ChE is the abbreviation for chemical engineer
SS is the steamship prefix

explanation.surface: A chemical engineer plays a game on board a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board ship' looks like one phrase, but the definition ends at 'board'. 'by' places the engineer next to the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess is the strategy game played with pieces on a chequered board of sixty-four squares.
